en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Confession (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on False Speech, 6.
The Second Training Rule on Sleeping Together.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, while the Venerable Anuruddha was traveling from the Kosala country toward Sāvatthī, he arrived at a certain village in the evening.
At that time, a guest house had been prepared by a certain woman in that village.
Then the Venerable Anuruddha approached that woman and said to her, “Sister, if it is not troublesome for you, we would like to stay one night in the guest house.”
“We would stay, venerable sir,” they replied.
Other travelers also approached that woman; having approached, they said to her, “If it is not troublesome for you, noble lady, we would stay one night in the guest house.
She replied, “Noble sirs, this ascetic arrived first; if he permits it, you may stay.”

Then those travelers approached the Venerable Anuruddha; having approached, they said this to the Venerable Anuruddha: "If it is not troublesome for you, venerable sir, we would stay for one night in the guest house.
"You may stay, friends," he replied.
Then that woman became bound by a heart of attachment at the mere sight of the Venerable Anuruddha.
Then that woman approached the Venerable Anuruddha; having approached, she said this to the Venerable Anuruddha: “Venerable sir, the noble one will not dwell in comfort being crowded by these people.
It would be well, venerable sir, if I were to prepare a couch for the noble one in the inner quarters.
The Venerable Anuruddha consented by remaining silent.

Then that woman, having prepared a couch for the Venerable Anuruddha within [the house], adorned and arrayed herself, fragrant with perfumes, approached the Venerable Anuruddha. Having approached, she said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
"Venerable sir, the noble one is handsome, beautiful, and pleasing; and I too am handsome, beautiful, and pleasing."
“Venerable sir, may I become the wife of this noble one.
When this was said, the Venerable Anuruddha remained silent.
A second time also... [as before]... he remained silent.
A third time, that woman said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
"Venerable sir, the noble one is handsome, beautiful, and pleasing; and I too am handsome, beautiful, and pleasing.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the noble one would accept me and all my property."
A third time, the Venerable Anuruddha remained silent.
Then that woman, having laid aside her garment, walked back and forth, stood, sat down, and even lay down right in front of the Venerable Anuruddha.
Yet the Venerable Anuruddha, having withdrawn his senses, neither looked at that woman nor spoke to her.
Then that woman thought: “It is wonderful indeed, it is marvelous indeed!
Many people send for me by the hundreds and by the thousands;
yet this ascetic, though entreated by me in person, does not wish to accept even me or all my property.”
Having put on her upper garment, she prostrated with her head at the feet of the Venerable Anuruddha and said this to him:
“Venerable sir, a transgression overcame me, in that I acted so foolishly, so deludedly, and so unskillfully.
May the noble sir accept my transgression as a transgression for the sake of future restraint.”
“Truly, sister, a transgression has overcome you, as was foolish, deluded, and unwholesome, in that you acted thus.
But since you, sister, having seen your transgression as a transgression, make amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it from you.

For this, sister, is growth in the discipline of the Noble One: that one who sees a transgression as a transgression makes amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma and undertakes restraint for the future.”
Then, at the end of that night, that woman, having personally satisfied and served the Venerable Anuruddha with excellent hard and soft foods,
and having bowed down to the Venerable Anuruddha after he had finished his meal and withdrawn his hand from the bowl,
sat down to one side.
As that woman was sitting to one side, the Venerable Anuruddha instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened her with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Venerable Anuruddha’s discourse on the Dhamma, that woman said to the Venerable Anuruddha:
“Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante!”

"Just as, venerable sir, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
even so has the Dhamma been elucidated by the noble Anuruddha in many ways.
Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."
“Venerable sir, may the Master accept me as a female lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
Then the Venerable Anuruddha went to Sāvatthī and reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [as before] ...were indignant, disparaged him, and complained, saying:
“How indeed could the Venerable Anuruddha share a sleeping place with a woman?
Then those monks, having rebuked the Venerable Anuruddha in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One asked:
“Is it true, Anuruddha, that you shared a sleeping place with a woman?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him: “… How, Anuruddha, can you lie down in the same bed with a woman?
This, Anuruddha, is neither for the inspiration of those without confidence nor for the increase of those who have confidence…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
“Whatever monk should share a sleeping place with a woman, that is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
“Whatever monk” means:
Whoever is such a one ... [as described] ...
"a bhikkhu" ...
this is what is intended by the term "bhikkhu" in this context.
"Woman" means a human female, not a *yakkhī*, not a *petī*, not one belonging to the animal realm; even a girl born on that very day is included, let alone one who is older.
"Together" means...
On one side.
What is called "a bed" (seyyā) is entirely covered, entirely enclosed, mostly covered, or mostly enclosed.
"He might lie down" means:
when the sun has set,
if a monk lies down while a woman is lying down, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If a woman lies down while a bhikkhu is already lying down, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If both lie down together, there is an offense of expiation.
If they rise up and lie down again and again, there is an offense of expiation for each instance.
If, perceiving a woman as a woman, one shares a sleeping place with her, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If, being doubtful about a woman, one shares a sleeping place with her, there is an offense of expiation.
If, perceiving a woman as not a woman, one shares a sleeping place with her, there is an offense of expiation.
If it is half-covered and half-enclosed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one shares a sleeping place with a female yakkha, a female peta, a paṇḍaka, or a female animal, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not a woman and one perceives her as a woman, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one is in doubt regarding whether it is a woman, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is not a woman and one perceives her as not being a woman, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
Completely covered and completely open;
completely open and completely covered;
mostly uncovered.
For the most part, when it is uncovered,
the monk sits while the woman lies down,
or the woman sits while the monk lies down.
Or both sit down; [it is not an offense] for one who is insane,
or for an initial offender.
The sixth training rule concerning sleeping in the same room with another person is finished.
